This article focuses on declarative Waydroid configuration on NixOS, an in-depth explanation of module options, the boundary between imperative and declarative management, and NixOS-specific troubleshooting. For the general installation process and architecture, first read Architecture in depth and the Multi-distribution installation guide.
NixOS module options in detail

The NixOS virtualisation.waydroid module encapsulates Waydroid installation, systemd service management, and network backend selection as declarative options. Understanding what each option means and how it maps to the underlying system is essential to configuring it correctly.

What the enable option does underneath
When you set virtualisation.waydroid.enable = true, the NixOS module does the following:
Installs the package: adds config.virtualisation.waydroid.package (selected by default according to the firewall configuration) to environment.systemPackages
Enables the systemd service: activates waydroid-container.service, which manages the lifecycle of the Android LXC container
Integrates D-Bus: registers the selected package's D-Bus files. The service BusName is id.waydro.Container. Check the D-Bus policy for actual authorization; do not invent a PolicyKit action

Checks kernel requirements: the 26.05 module checks ANDROID_BINDER_IPC, ANDROID_BINDERFS, and MEMFD_CREATE, and adds psi=1. The module itself does not declare the described modprobe ExecStartPre; driver probing is handled by the actual package/upstream process.

enable = true does not automatically run waydroid init. Downloading and initializing the images must be done manually. See the section "The boundary between imperative and declarative management" below.
The package option: iptables vs. nftables variants
This is one of the most important options on NixOS. nixpkgs provides two Waydroid derivations:
Derivation
Network backend
Use case
Older systems using iptables firewall rules, or situations with an explicit compatibility requirement
Configurations with networking.nftables.enable enabled

Technical background: Waydroid needs a NAT network to give the Android container access to external networks. Early Waydroid versions used iptables rules for NAT, but as the Linux ecosystem moved toward nftables, upstream Waydroid added nftables support. nixpkgs supports these backends through two separate derivations, which differ in their build-time dependencies and bundled network scripts:
pkgs.waydroid: depends on iptables and uses the iptables command to create NAT and DNAT rules
pkgs.waydroid-nftables: depends on nftables and uses the nft command to create equivalent nftables rules
How to choose
First check the current networking.nftables.enable setting; do not infer that it is enabled from the NixOS version number.
If your NixOS configuration explicitly sets networking.nftables.enable = false and still uses iptables, you can fall back to pkgs.waydroid.
These packages integrate different network backends. Their actual interaction with host rules still needs verification; identical behavior in every respect is not guaranteed.
How the module maps to systemd services
Waydroid on NixOS involves two levels of systemd service:

The key distinction: waydroid-container.service is a system-level systemd service started by multi-user.target (or manually). waydroid-session is a user-session-level service and must run in a graphical session (Wayland). They communicate over D-Bus, with PolicyKit controlling permissions.

Supported Android images can use memfd instead of the old ashmem path. This is not a replacement for Binder or a guarantee of improved performance:

The boundary between imperative and declarative management

The most important concept when using Waydroid on NixOS is this: the existing module manages system-side configuration, while Android images and application data retain their own state. Understanding this boundary keeps you from the dead end of trying to "put everything in Nix".
Why it cannot be completely declarative
There is a fundamental tension between Waydroid's runtime model and NixOS's declarative philosophy:
There are three central tensions:

Downloading images is a network side effect: waydroid init downloads Android system images (about 300-500MB) from sourceforge.net or ota.waydro.id, which is a network I/O operation. Ordinary builds restrict network access, but fixed-output fetchers can retrieve images by hash. Whether to manage this through Nix is a matter of engineering design and update strategy.

Image updates are ongoing external events: OTA updates follow upstream releases and are not guaranteed weekly. You can record the image channel, version, and hash, or even define a custom pinned source, but the existing NixOS module does not do this automatically.

Initialization writes to runtime directories: waydroid init extracts images into /var/lib/waydroid/ (system level) and writes configuration files to ~/.local/share/waydroid/ (user level). These paths are outside the Nix store (/nix/store/) and are not protected by NixOS's atomicity.

Community discussions and design judgments

The source notes provide no verifiable discussion links, so their English quotations and claims of “unanimous consensus” cannot be treated as actual community conclusions. In a real design, distinguish configuration, image inputs, and user data. The first two can be versioned or hash-pinned as needed; the last still requires backups and migration. Rolling back a system generation does not automatically roll back /var/lib/waydroid or user data.

NixOS-specific problems and solutions

NixOS's immutable infrastructure model and distinctive system organization can cause problems that do not arise on other distributions. The following are the most common failure scenarios for NixOS users and their solutions.
Issue 1: fstab warnings — "Do not install Waydroid before running nixos-generate-config"
Symptoms:
Or, more seriously:

Cause: Waydroid's systemd service creates bind mounts under /var/lib/waydroid/. nixos-generate-config scans /proc/mounts and writes all mount points to hardware-configuration.nix. If the Waydroid container is running at that point, the generated configuration incorrectly includes Waydroid's internal mounts.
Solution:
Best practice: complete the initial NixOS installation and run nixos-generate-config before installing Waydroid. If you have already encountered this problem, the cleanup steps above can resolve it.
Issue 2: LXC version mismatch
Symptoms:

Cause: Waydroid and LXC in nixpkgs may have mismatched versions because channel updates are out of sync. Waydroid depends heavily on the LXC user-space toolchain (lxc-start, lxc-stop, and others). Incompatible versions can prevent the container from starting.

Solution:

On the NixOS unstable channel, LXC and Waydroid version discrepancies are usually fixed through PRs within a few days. If you encounter this problem, try reverting to the previous channel version or waiting for an update.
Issue 3: the binder kernel module is unavailable
Symptoms:
Cause: the NixOS kernel builds binder_linux as a module by default, but some custom kernel configurations may omit the ANDROID_BINDER_IPC option.
Diagnosis:
Solution (NixOS):

NixOS 26.05 (kernel 6.18.x) includes ANDROID_BINDER_IPC=m by default, so additional configuration is usually unnecessary. If you use a nonstandard kernel (such as linux_lqx or linux_zen), confirm that it includes this option.
Issue 4: compositor compatibility and optional nested sessions
Symptoms: after starting Waydroid on Hyprland, the window does not display correctly or input events behave erratically.

Cause: Waydroid runs as a standalone window under Wayland, but some Wayland compositors, especially wlroots-based Hyprland, may conflict with Waydroid's Wayland backend in window compositing or input-focus management.
Solution: use cage to create a nested Wayland session:

If you use GNOME Wayland or KDE Plasma Wayland, cage is usually unnecessary. Whether a nested session is needed depends on the specific version and problem. Hyprland is not currently a wlroots-based project, so it should not be categorized that way generally.
Issue 5: hybrid-GPU multi-output configuration
Symptoms: on laptops with hybrid graphics (Intel + NVIDIA / AMD + NVIDIA), Waydroid may select the wrong GPU.

Cause: hybrid graphics on NixOS are usually managed through hardware.nvidia.prime (NVIDIA PRIME) or services.xserver.videoDrivers. Waydroid detects GPUs through render nodes under /dev/dri/ (renderD128, renderD129, and so on), and may select the wrong node.

Summary
Core principles for deploying Waydroid on NixOS:

Manage declaratively what you can: package installation, systemd services, environment variables, and PolicyKit rules, all configured declaratively through virtualisation.waydroid and systemd options.

Keep the unavoidable imperative operations separate: wrap waydroid init, waydroid upgrade, and waydroid prop set in one-time scripts or systemd timers, maintaining a clear boundary with the NixOS configuration.
Choose the correct backend: select a consistent backend based on networking.nftables.enable and the actual package.
Prefer integrated graphics: GBM mode with AMD/Intel open-source drivers provides the best experience; NVIDIA users need special handling.
Use community resources: waydroid-helper (NixOS 25.11+) and NUR's waydroid-script can simplify common operations.

Waydroid's "incomplete declarative support" is not a flaw in NixOS. It is the boundary of the existing module and runtime-state management. Accepting that boundary and bridging the gaps with scripts is the best practice for using NixOS and Waydroid together.
